evidence: src/domain/entities/Order.ts: the STATUS_ORDER constant is the only place the status order is defined. canTransitionTo uses it, and transitionTo calls canTransitionTo as its guard.
src/domain/entities/Product.ts: getAvailableStock() works out totalStock - reservedStock in one place. canReserve uses it, and reserve calls canReserve as its guard.
Both entities follow the same guard-then-mutate pattern (canTransitionTo/transitionTo and canReserve/reserve), so the abstraction is consistent.
src/domain/entities/Order.ts: OrderLine { productId: string; quantity: number } refers to Product by id only, so the entity boundaries stay separate.
src/domain/entities/Order.ts: canBeCancelled() lists the statuses 'shipped' and 'delivered' by name. This is a separate cancellation rule in the same file, not a duplicated invariant.
parsedVerdict.reasoning:
The module holds two domain entity classes, Order and Product. Together they cover one concern: the core entities of the order domain. Each class keeps its own invariants in one place.
- Order owns the status lifecycle. The allowed order of statuses is the STATUS_ORDER array, which canTransitionTo uses and transitionTo enforces.
- Product owns stock reservation. The available-stock rule is in getAvailableStock, which canReserve uses and reserve enforces.
The two files use the same style: private state, guard methods (canX) and mutators that throw when their guard fails. Neither repeats a rule from the other or reaches into the other's internals. OrderLine refers to a product only through productId, so the two entities stay separate. One small point: canBeCancelled lists 'shipped' and 'delivered' by name instead of working them out from STATUS_ORDER. This is a separate cancellation rule kept in the same file, not a repeated copy of an invariant, so it does not fail the rubric.
